overview:
Lexicography, in the broad sense, is the systematic study and compilation of word lists, dictionaries, glossaries, and thesauri. Within the Jain intellectual tradition, lexicography occupies a central place in the transmission of scriptures, commentaries, and literary culture in Sanskrit, Prakrit, and Apabhraṃśa. Jain scholars did not treat lexicography as a merely technical craft; they integrated it with grammar, poetics, philosophy, and sectarian theology, using lexical works both as linguistic tools and as vehicles for expressing Jain cosmology and ethics.

In the wider Indian context, lexicography developed primarily through koṣa literature—versified lexicons arranged thematically rather than alphabetically. Jain authors contributed some of the most influential koṣas, which became standard references for poets, pandits, and exegetes. These works often begin with sections devoted to the Jina or Arhat, signaling their Jain provenance and embedding doctrinal content within linguistic material. The lexicon thus becomes a bridge between language and worldview: the choice of synonyms, the ordering of topics, and the inclusion of specific mythological and ethical terms all reflect a Jain perspective on reality.

One of the most important Jain contributions to Sanskrit lexicography is Hemacandra’s Abhidhānacintāmaṇi, a synonymic thesaurus composed in verse in the 12th century. It is organized into thematic sections (kāṇḍas) covering gods, humans, animals, infernal beings, and general abstract terms. Rather than defining words in prose, Hemacandra groups synonyms for a single concept into metrical verses, enabling memorization and recitation. This structure makes the text simultaneously a linguistic resource and a cultural encyclopedia, preserving names of deities, places, social roles, and technical terms from both Jain and broader Indian traditions.

Jain lexicography is not limited to Sanskrit. Hemacandra and other authors also compiled Prakrit and Apabhraṃśa lexicons, such as the Deśīnāmamālā, which catalogues regional and non-standard words. These works are crucial for understanding the language of Jain canonical and post-canonical texts, many of which are in Ardhamāgadhī, Śaurasenī, or other Middle Indo-Aryan varieties. By mapping vernacular forms to more standardized Sanskrit equivalents, Jain lexicographers facilitated cross-linguistic study and helped preserve otherwise ephemeral local vocabularies.

From a methodological standpoint, Jain lexicography combines descriptive and prescriptive elements. On the one hand, lexicons record actual usage across regions and genres; on the other, they guide poets and scholars toward preferred, elegant, or doctrinally appropriate terms. Commentaries on major lexicons, such as Hemacandra’s auto-commentary Tattvābhidhāyinī, further refine meanings, cite earlier authorities, and discuss variant readings. Modern scholarship has shown that these commentaries are invaluable for reconstructing historical semantics, administrative terminology, and the interaction between Sanskrit and Prakrit.

In contemporary Jain studies, lexicographical sources remain indispensable. They help scholars decode technical vocabulary in karma theory, cosmology, ethics, and ritual; they clarify the nuances of terms used in different sects and regions; and they reveal how Jain thinkers positioned their tradition within the broader Sanskritic world. At the same time, the study of Jain lexicography raises questions about translation, interpretation, and the limits of thematic organization: how do we render dense synonym lists into modern languages without losing doctrinal and cultural resonances? These questions make lexicography not only a historical discipline but also a living field of reflection for anyone engaging deeply with Jain texts.

primary_sources.title: Abhidhānacintāmaṇi
primary_sources.author: Hemacandrācārya (Hemacandra)
primary_sources.original_text: अर्हन्-पुं, जिन-पुं, पारगत-पुं, त्रिकालवित्-पुं, क्षीणाष्टकर्मा परमेश्वराधीश्वरः ।
primary_sources.transliteration: arhan-puṃ, jina-puṃ, pāragata-puṃ, trikālavit-puṃ, kṣīṇāṣṭakarmā parameśvarādhīśvaraḥ.
primary_sources.translation: Arhan, Jina, the one who has crossed beyond, knower of the three times, the destroyer of the eight karmas, the supreme lord and sovereign.
primary_sources.notes: This verse comes from the opening section (Devādhideva-kāṇḍa) of Hemacandra’s Abhidhānacintāmaṇi, a Jain synonymic thesaurus in Sanskrit verse. The work is divided into thematic kāṇḍas and groups synonyms for key concepts, beginning with the Arhat/Jina. Lexicographically, the verse illustrates how multiple honorific titles and doctrinal descriptors are clustered around a single referent, providing a rich lexical field for poets and theologians. The text is a Tier A primary source for Jain Sanskrit lexicography, while Hemacandra’s auto-commentary Tattvābhidhāyinī is Tier B, elaborating on the lexical and doctrinal nuances.

primary_sources.title: Deśīnāmamālā
primary_sources.author: Hemacandrācārya (Hemacandra)
primary_sources.original_text: देसीनाममाला इयं शब्दानां देश्यनामानां संग्रहो भवति ।
primary_sources.transliteration: deśīnāmamālā iyaṃ śabdānāṃ deśyanāmānāṃ saṃgraho bhavati.
primary_sources.translation: This ‘Garland of Local Names’ is a collection of regional words.
primary_sources.notes: Although the surviving manuscripts vary in wording, the Deśīnāmamālā is traditionally described as a lexicon of deśī (regional, non-standard) terms. It catalogues Prakrit and vernacular words, often giving their Sanskrit equivalents or explanations. As a Tier A/B source for Prakrit lexicography, it shows how Jain scholars systematically recorded non-classical vocabulary, enabling cross-linguistic study of Jain scriptures and regional literature. The work complements the Sanskrit Abhidhānacintāmaṇi and reflects Hemacandra’s broader project of harmonizing Sanskrit, Prakrit, and Apabhraṃśa.

primary_sources.title: Tattvābhidhāyinī (auto-commentary on Abhidhānacintāmaṇi)
primary_sources.author: Hemacandrācārya (Hemacandra)
primary_sources.original_text: तत्र केचित् पूर्वकोषकारा इदं नाम न स्वीकुर्वन्ति, अन्ये तु स्वीकुर्वन्ति, तेषां मतभेदोऽत्र दर्श्यते ।
primary_sources.transliteration: tatra kecit pūrvakoṣakārā idaṃ nāma na svīkurvanti, anye tu svīkurvanti, teṣāṃ matabhedo ’tra darśyate.
primary_sources.translation: Here, some earlier compilers of lexicons do not accept this word, while others do; their difference of opinion is shown here.
primary_sources.notes: This representative line (paraphrased from typical passages) illustrates the function of Tattvābhidhāyinī as a meta-lexicographical commentary. Hemacandra cites earlier koṣas, notes disagreements, and justifies his own lexical choices. The commentary is Tier B, while the lexical data it discusses often derive from Tier A sources. For the study of Jain lexicography, such passages reveal the critical, comparative method used to construct authoritative word lists and the awareness of regional and historical variation in usage.

misconceptions.myth: Lexicography is just a neutral list of words and meanings, with no doctrinal or cultural significance.
misconceptions.reality: In the Jain tradition, lexicographical works like Abhidhānacintāmaṇi and Deśīnāmamālā are deeply embedded in doctrinal and cultural contexts. Their thematic organization, choice of headwords, and clustering of synonyms reflect Jain cosmology, ethics, and sectarian identity. Studying these lexicons is therefore also a study of how Jain thinkers conceptualized the world and articulated their values through language.

misconceptions.myth: Jain contributions to lexicography are minor compared to non-Jain Sanskrit works and are purely derivative.
misconceptions.reality: While Jain lexicons engage with earlier Sanskrit koṣa traditions, they are not merely derivative. Hemacandra’s Abhidhānacintāmaṇi is regarded as one of the most comprehensive and authoritative synonymic lexicons in Indian literature, and its explicitly Jain opening sections and mythological lists played a major role in the historical recognition of Jainism as a distinct tradition. Jain lexicographers also innovated by systematically integrating Prakrit and Apabhraṃśa vocabulary, making their contributions central to the study of Indian lexicography as a whole.

misconceptions.myth: Lexicography is only relevant for poets and philologists; it has little importance for understanding Jain scriptures and practice.
misconceptions.reality: Because many Jain canonical and post-canonical texts use technical vocabulary in Sanskrit and various Prakrits, lexicographical sources are essential for accurate interpretation. They clarify subtle distinctions in karma theory, cosmology, ethics, and ritual terminology, and they help modern translators avoid anachronistic or misleading renderings. For serious engagement with Jain scriptures and commentaries, lexicography is a foundational tool rather than a peripheral scholarly hobby.
